Dear Nilesh,
The result came on Thursday. I failed maths, the one paper everybody expected me to top. In the kitchen Papa went silent and Mummy cried without a sound. Half our building knows by now. I keep thinking my whole plan is finished and I have made everyone ashamed. I know that is probably not how things really are, but tonight it feels that way. This afternoon our class teacher, Kavita ma'am, phoned home and asked us to see the school counsellor together on Monday. Mummy said yes at once. I am writing to you because you failed once too, and I want to know how it got better.
Simran

subtype: Failing an exam and feeling finished [Actor]
passage: Gautam, you want to hear about the time I failed the board exam? Fine. I'm Jeevan. It was Class 10, physics. On result day I stared at the screen and thought that was it: no college, no future, everyone in the neighbourhood talking. I shut myself in my room. That same evening my uncle knocked, sat on the bed with two cups of tea and said nothing about marks. Then he said, "Tomorrow morning we'll talk to the school counsellor." We went. The counsellor listened and said that the feeling of "this is permanent" is common after a shock, and we planned the supplementary exam together. I still remember how heavy it was, and how it lifted a little.

In Singapore, the results came out at noon. Ada read the paper in the school hall and felt the floor tilt. She had failed maths. Not badly, but failed. Without it, the course she wanted was out of reach.
On the bus home, she stared out of the window. Her aunties would be at dinner on Sunday. Her cousins were all engineers. Her friend Xin texted, "How was it??" She didn't reply.
At home she shut her door and lay face down on the bed. Everything felt finished: the course, the plan, the version of herself she had pictured.
At six her mother knocked and came in without waiting. She sat on the bed and put a hand on Ada's back. "Xin's mother called. Tell me."
Ada cried for a long time. Her mother just listened. Then she said, "Tonight we eat. Tomorrow we find out about the retake. It hurts. It is not the end."

qa.q: What subject did Ada fail?
qa.a: She had failed maths.

qa.q: How did Ada feel lying face down on the bed?
qa.a: Ada felt hurt and hopeless, as if the course, the plan and her pictured future were all finished.

qa.q: What did Ada's mother do that helped that evening?
qa.a: Her mother came in, listened while Ada cried, and put the next step, finding out about the retake, off until tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Xin have felt when Ada didn't reply?
qa.a: Xin was probably worried, which is why Xin's mother called Ada's mother that evening.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who fails a major exam and feels her future has collapsed, while a parent's same-day support shows it is painful but not permanent.

subtype: Failing an exam and feeling finished [Actor]
passage:
On result day, the corridor outside the Class Ten staff room was loud with shrieks and phone calls. Devika stood near the water cooler, staring at her phone. Maths: 28. Fail.
She thought of her father telling the whole colony she would do science. Of her cousin who got ninety-five. She couldn't breathe properly. Her eyes blurred.
Mr Gurpreet Singh, the school counsellor, saw her and walked over. He didn't say "It's okay." He said, "Come sit with me for a bit." In his room, with the door open, he gave her water and waited.
"My life is over, sir," she whispered.
"It feels that way today. That feeling is real," he said. "But there's a supplementary exam in July. Many students pass it. You are more than this number."
Before she left, he asked for her mother's number and called her while Devika sat there. "She needs you to be kind to her today," he said.

qa.q: What did Devika score in maths?
qa.a: Maths: 28. Fail.

qa.q: How did Devika feel standing near the water cooler?
qa.a: Devika felt panicked and crushed, unable to breathe properly, thinking of her father's boasts and her cousin's marks.

qa.q: What did Mr Gurpreet Singh do well in that hour?
qa.a: He sat with Devika, accepted that the pain was real, told her about the supplementary exam and called her mother that same day to ask for kindness.

qa.q: How might Devika's mother feel after the counsellor's call?
qa.a: Her mother might feel worried but also guided, knowing to meet Devika with kindness rather than anger that evening.

grounding: Shows a teenager who fails a board exam and feels her future is over, and a counsellor who responds the same day with support and a next step.

Dear Kishore mama,
The Class Twelve results came out yesterday. I failed physics.
Everyone in our building knew I wanted engineering. Aunty from the second floor asked Amma, "So, which college?" and Amma just said, "Let's see." I heard it from my room. I felt like the whole building was looking at our door.
Last night I kept thinking my whole future was gone. That all my friends would move ahead and I'd be stuck. I told Amma I felt like that, and she sat with me till I slept. Today she took me to the school counsellor, who said I can take the compartment exam in July and still join college this year.
It still hurts. I'm writing because you once told me you failed your first year of college, and I never believed you. Was it true? Can I call you on Sunday?
Chinmay

qa.a: I failed physics.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when the neighbour asked Amma about college?
qa.a: Chinmay felt ashamed and exposed, as if the whole building was looking at their door.

qa.a: Kishore mama would probably feel touched and protective, glad Chinmay reached out and ready to share his own story.

subtype: Failing an exam and feeling finished [Actor]
passage:
Preeti, you're the only one I can say this to. When the board results came out, I saw "Fail" next to maths and my whole body went cold. Every other kid in my building passed. Sharma aunty had already sent sweets around for her son. Papa had told everyone at the shop I'd get science stream. I thought, that's it, Parul, you're finished. No science, no college, no job, everyone laughing.
I didn't eat. I lay facing the wall. Around ten, Mummy came and sat on my bed and didn't say a word about marks. She just held my hand and said, "We'll look at the compartment exam tomorrow, not tonight."
Today my tuition sir said lots of students clear it in July. I don't fully believe it yet. But it's been four days, and the world hasn't ended, even if it still feels a bit like it.

qa.q: What did Mummy say when she sat on the bed?
qa.a: "We'll look at the compartment exam tomorrow, not tonight."

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when the result came?
qa.a: Parul felt shocked and hopeless, body going cold, sure that one failed subject meant no science, no college and everyone laughing.

qa.q: What could help Parul in the days ahead?
qa.a: Taking one small step, like finding out about the July compartment exam with the tuition teacher, and keeping on talking to Mummy or Preeti when it feels heavy.

qa.q: Why might Mummy have avoided talking about marks that night?
qa.a: Mummy probably saw how hurt Parul was and chose comfort first, leaving the plans for the next day.
